q: Does the 'R19/R21/R23 straddle the 95% ANI species cutoff' finding hold at the paper's full 128-reference-genome scale, or does denser sampling of flavescens/perflava/subflava reference space collapse them cleanly onto one species?
basis: This replication used a stratified 15-reference subset (2-3 per relevant species) rather than the paper's 128 references. Within that subset, R19 hits N. subflava C2005001510 at 98.04% and N. perflava 27098_8_142 at 98.05%, both higher than any hit to a labeled N. flavescens reference (max 94.08%). If the paper's larger reference set contains flavescens strains with ANI >=95% to R19 that our subset missed, the flavescens assignment could still be valid at full scale. Conversely, a full-scale rerun could show the flavescens/perflava/subflava reference cluster is itself internally sub-95% ANI, in which case the entire species trio is under-delineated.
next_steps: Fetch all 128 accessions listed in the paper's Table S1 via NCBI datasets, rerun skani triangle mode, and produce the same UPGMA tree. Compare the species-level connected components at the 95% ANI cutoff to the paper's OrthoANI-based species assignments row-by-row.

q: What fraction of NCBI RefSeq Neisseria genomes fail a strict >=95%-ANI-to-deposited-species-type-strain sanity check? The paper claims 'many' errors and shows one example (VK64/sicca actually macacae); a systematic audit would quantify the base rate.
basis: In our 15-reference subset, one genome (GCF_000260655.1, deposited as N. sicca VK64) was 96.83% ANI to N. macacae, i.e. mislabeled by the paper's own criteria. That is 1/15 = 6.7% of a small sample. If the full Neisseria RefSeq collection (~400-600 assemblies as of 2026) has a comparable or higher error rate, it is a directly quantifiable, actionable finding for NCBI curation.
next_steps: Download all NCBI RefSeq Neisseria assemblies plus canonical type-strain assemblies for each Neisseria species. Run skani all-vs-type-strains. Report percentage of assemblies whose top >=95% ANI hit disagrees with the deposited species name, stratified by species and by assembly submission year.

q: Is the low R19/R23 (94.32%) and R21/R23 (94.58%) pairwise ANI a real biological signal (three subspecies-divergent commensal Neisseria co-isolated from a single-country sampling window) or an artifact of the paper's A5-pipeline draft-assembly quality (contig counts 34, 36, 79 respectively)?
basis: R23's assembly has 79 contigs (vs 34 for R19, 36 for R21). Draft-assembly fragmentation with different contig sets can cause skani/OrthoANI to align slightly different portions of the same genome and mildly bias ANI downward. However, R19-R21 at 95.50% (both low contig count) and R19-R23 at 94.32% suggest a genuine ~1 percentage-point separation beyond what contig count alone predicts.
next_steps: Re-download the raw Illumina reads (ENA/SRA accessions from paper's PRJEB30649 project), reassemble R19/R21/R23 with SPAdes or Unicycler under identical parameters (equalizing contig quality), and rerun skani. If the 94-95% ANI structure persists, it is biological.

q: The paper never states which decision rule takes precedence when 'closest species' and 'strict >=95% ANI cutoff' disagree. What is the actual decision procedure they used, and would applying the strict cutoff consistently change their reported assignments?
basis: Section 4.3 says '95% ANI cutoff' but Section 3 (Results) assigns species by closest match. Our replication finds these two rules give different answers for R19/R21/R23 (closest-flavescens-reference vs any >=95%-hit-anywhere). Making the decision rule explicit is a methodological reproducibility gap that any downstream user of the paper's assignments would need resolved.
next_steps: Re-derive the paper's Table 3 (isDDH values) with the exact rule 'assign species = highest isDDH iff isDDH >= 70%, else Neisseria sp.' and compare to the paper's assignments. Where they diverge, flag as ambiguous.

q: The paper reports that OrthoANI + isDDH + Roary pangenome 'together' are the best identifier, but does not quantify inter-tool disagreement. On the same 19-genome test set, how often do the three tools produce the same species assignment for each isolate, and what would a fourth tool (skani, GTDB-Tk classify, or a phylogenetic placement like autoMLST) add or subtract?
basis: Our replication reran only ANI (skani); Mash was consistent qualitatively. The paper's 'combination is best' claim is not testable from ANI alone. A four-tool concordance study on R19/R20/R21/R23 would either strengthen the paper's methodological claim (all four agree in obvious cases, split predictably at ambiguous cases) or weaken it (>1 tool disagrees systematically, e.g., pangenome puts R19 with flavescens while ANI puts it with subflava).
next_steps: Run all four tools (skani ANI, GGDC isDDH via web, Roary pangenome on Prokka-annotated genomes, GTDB-Tk classify_wf) on the same 19-genome set. Score each isolate on all four; report a per-isolate concordance vector; compute Fleiss' kappa across tools.
